screens.title: Raycasting and Linecasting for Interaction
screens.subtitle: Query the physics world without physical contact to detect objects, surfaces, and distances instantly.

narration.text: In this lesson we will learn how to use raycasting and linecasting to ask questions of the physics world without creating physical objects. Raycasting is like shining an invisible laser from a point in a direction and receiving a report about what it hits. You will learn the primary Unity A P I, how to read the returned RaycastHit data, how to filter results with LayerMask, and concrete scenarios where raycasts are the right tool: shooting, object selection, line of sight checks, and ground detection. We will also contrast linecasting and thicker casts such as sphere and box casts so you know when to expand a ray into a volume. By the end you will be able to implement a mouse-based selector, a grounded check for a character, and debug rays inside the Scene view. One practical tip you will carry forward is to treat raycasts as queries — fast, non-physical checks that rely on colliders being present. Ready to explore how invisible queries power common gameplay interactions and debugging workflows?

keyIdea.title: Why use raycasts?
keyIdea.text: Raycasts let you detect colliders instantly without physics simulation, enabling precise hits, selection, and line-of-sight checks.

screens.title: What is Raycasting?
screens.subtitle: A clear definition and practical mental model

narration.text: Raycasting is a non-physical query of the physics world. Think of it as shining an invisible, instantaneous laser from an origin in a direction and asking the physics engine, did that beam encounter any colliders within a given distance? If the ray intersects a collider, the engine returns a populated RaycastHit with details about the impact. Unlike collision events, raycasts do not require a Rigidbody on the casting object and they do not cause forces or responses. They rely on the presence of colliders to report hits. A concrete example is detecting what the player is looking at: cast a ray from the camera through the center of the screen and, if the ray returns a hit, use the hit's transform to highlight or interact. A common misconception is that a ray will affect physics; it will not. Another contrast is between raycasts and physical projectiles: a projectile simulates movement and can bounce or trigger collision messages, whereas a raycast simply reports whether a path is blocked. Key takeaway: use raycasts to ask questions about the world quickly and deterministically without adding objects to the simulation. How will you apply that pattern in your next interaction mechanic?

keyIdea.title: Raycasting defined
keyIdea.text: A fast, non-physical query that detects colliders along a line and returns detailed hit data if a collision occurs.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › What is Raycasting?
Definition and mental model
Raycasting: an instantaneous query that reports the first collider intersected along a direction. No physics interactions are produced by the ray itself.
When to use it
  • Player look-at selection and clicking on objects.
  • Instant hit detection for weapons with visual-only bullets.
  • Line-of-sight checks for AI agents.
Common misconception
Rays do not apply forces or trigger rigidbody collisions. They only report information when they intersect colliders.
Key Takeaway

Use raycasts for fast, deterministic detection when no physical projectile or force is required.

Concrete example
Cast a ray from the camera through the mouse position. If it hits an object, change its material color to highlight it. The ray provides a hit point and the transform for identification.
Check your understanding
  • Define raycasting in your own words and name one situation where it is preferable to a physical projectile.
  • Explain why a collider is required on the target for the ray to report a hit.

screens.title: Using Physics.Raycast
screens.subtitle: Parameters, overloads, and the typical call pattern

narration.text: The common Physics. Raycast call pattern takes an origin point, a direction vector, an output RaycastHit, a maximum distance, and an optional LayerMask. When you call Physics. Raycast with these parameters, the engine performs a single line test and returns true if any collider is intersected within the given range. A reliable process is: normalize the direction vector so maxDistance scales predictably; provide an out RaycastHit variable and only access its fields if the call returns true; and set a sensible max distance to limit scope and improve performance. For examples, you may use Camera. ScreenPointToRay for mouse selection or transform. forward when firing from a weapon. Remember that Physics. Raycast has multiple overloads: you can pass a Ray struct directly, or provide origin and direction separately. Each overload serves convenience; the core behavior is the same. A frequent mistake is forgetting the out keyword, which will fail compilation, and another is not normalizing the direction, which can make maxDistance behave inconsistently. Try a short read-evaluate-debug loop: call the raycast, inspect RaycastHit, and draw the ray using Debug. DrawRay to verify direction and distance visually. What guard will you add to avoid null access after a failed raycast?

keyIdea.title: Raycast pattern
keyIdea.text: Normalize direction, call Physics.Raycast with an out RaycastHit, check the boolean result before reading hit data, and limit maxDistance.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Physics.Raycast
Call pattern
Origin, direction, out RaycastHit, maxDistance, and LayerMask. Normalize direction and guard access with the returned boolean.
Steps
  1. Create origin and direction vectors and normalize direction.
  2. Declare RaycastHit hit; call Physics.Raycast and check the bool result.
  3. If true, read hit.point, hit.normal, hit.collider, or hit.transform.
Common mistakes
  • Forgetting the out keyword when declaring RaycastHit.
  • Using an unnormalized direction and misinterpreting maxDistance.
  • Attempting to access hit fields when the ray returned false.
Code example (visual only)
// Create a ray from the camera through the mouse Ray ray = Camera.main.ScreenPointToRay(Input.mousePosition); RaycastHit hit; if (Physics.Raycast(ray, out hit, maxSelectionDistance, selectableLayers)) { // Use hit.transform, hit.point, hit.normal } // Debug.DrawRay(ray.origin, ray.direction * maxSelectionDistance, Color.red);
Pro tip

Prefer specifying maxDistance and LayerMask to reduce unnecessary checks and improve performance in dense scenes.

screens.title: The Ray and RaycastHit Structures
screens.subtitle: What each field means and how to use them in logic

narration.text: Understanding the Ray and RaycastHit structures is central to using raycasts effectively. A Ray consists of an origin and a direction vector. The direction should normally be a unit vector so that distance behaves consistently. The RaycastHit struct is populated when a raycast succeeds and contains several fields you will use regularly. The collider field provides the Collider component that was hit; this is useful to disable or query specific properties. The rigidbody field gives you the Rigidbody if the hit object has one, letting you apply forces or change physics state if needed. The transform field is a convenient shortcut to position or name the hit object. The point field is the exact world position of intersection; use it to place effects or determine impact coordinates. The normal describes the surface orientation at the hit point, which is valuable for reflection calculations or aligning decals. The distance is the scalar from the ray origin to the hit point. A common error is to read these fields without checking the raycast result; always guard them. For example, when implementing shooting, read hit. point to spawn an impact effect at the right position and use hit. normal to orient it. What will you do first with hit. point in your next prototype?

keyIdea.title: Hit data explained
keyIdea.text: RaycastHit provides collider, rigidbody, transform, point, normal, and distance — the core data you need to react to a detected hit.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Ray & RaycastHit
Ray: origin and direction
Construct a Ray with an origin and a direction. Normalize the direction for predictable distance checks.
origin
World position where the ray starts.
direction
Unit vector describing the ray's path.
RaycastHit fields
Use these values only when Physics.Raycast returns true.
point
Exact world position of impact; spawn effects here.
normal
Surface orientation at the hit; useful for reflection or decals.
collider / transform / rigidbody
References to the hit object's components for identification or physics interaction.
distance
Distance from origin to impact; useful for range-limited effects.
Example use

Spawn an impact decal at hit.point and orient it with hit.normal so it sits flush with the surface.

screens.title: LayerMask: Filtering Raycasts
screens.subtitle: Bitmask basics and common patterns for inclusion and exclusion

narration.text: LayerMask is a bitmask used to select which layers a raycast will consider. This is essential for both accuracy and performance. To construct a mask, convert layer names to their bit index and combine them with bit shifts. For example, shifting one by a player layer index and combining it with an enemy layer gives a mask that hits only those layers. You can also invert a mask to hit everything except a particular layer, which is useful when you want to ignore a group such as effects or triggers. A concrete scenario: you want your selection ray to ignore UI and visual-only colliders, so configure selectableLayers in the Inspector and pass it into Physics. Raycast. A common pitfall is confusing a LayerMask variable shown in the Inspector with the raw integer bitmask; use the Inspector field to pick layers or construct the mask with bit operators. When debugging, temporarily set the mask to include everything to confirm your ray logic works, then tighten the mask to the necessary layers. Finally, remember that improper masks can make rays silently ignore intended targets — always verify layer assignments on the GameObjects you expect to hit.

keyIdea.title: LayerMask function
keyIdea.text: LayerMask controls which layers a ray will hit; use bit shifts to combine layers and invert to exclude specific layers.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › LayerMask Filtering
Bitmask basics
Build masks by shifting 1 by a layer index and combining with bitwise OR. Invert masks with bitwise NOT to exclude layers.
int playerLayer = LayerMask.NameToLayer("Player"); int enemyLayer = LayerMask.NameToLayer("Enemy"); int mask = (1 << playerLayer) | (1 << enemyLayer); // Exclude a layer: int ignore = LayerMask.NameToLayer("IgnoreRaycast"); int allExcept = ~(1 << ignore);
Practical tip

Expose LayerMask fields in the Inspector and select layers visually to avoid bit-shift errors in code.

Example scenario
A mouse selector should only hit objects on a SelectableObjects layer. Assign scene objects to that layer and set the selectableLayers mask on the MouseSelector component so clicks ignore everything else.
Debug checklist
  • Confirm object layer assignments in the Inspector.
  • Temporarily widen the mask to include all layers for testing.
  • Then tighten the mask to the intended layers only.

screens.title: Mouse-Based Selection Example
screens.subtitle: Walk through the MouseSelector script and expected behavior

narration.text: Let's walk through the MouseSelector example that highlights objects under the cursor. The script casts a ray from the camera through the mouse position using Camera. ScreenPointToRay and stores the result in a RaycastHit out variable. If Physics. Raycast returns true, it sets the currentSelection to the hit transform and highlights it by changing the renderer's material color. The script must restore the original color each frame if the selection changes, so keep a stored originalColor. The public LayerMask selectableLayers controls which objects respond to the ray. A concrete run-through: move the mouse over an object assigned to SelectableObjects. The script casts a ray, finds the collider, and sets the object's color to yellow. Click to trigger a debug log that prints the hit. transform. name and hit. point. Common pitfalls include not having a Collider on the target, forgetting to set the LayerMask in the Inspector, or accessing renderer material without checking for null. Always guard those operations. After you implement this, run the scene and use Debug. DrawRay to visualize the ray in the Scene view and make sure it aligns with your cursor and max distance. What will you log the first time you click an object?

keyIdea.title: Selection pattern
keyIdea.text: Cast a camera ray through the mouse, check Physics.Raycast with a LayerMask, highlight the hit object's renderer, and log the hit point.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › MouseSelector Walkthrough
MouseSelector logic
Reset previous highlight, cast a ray from Camera.ScreenPointToRay, check Raycast result, store original color, and change to highlight color.
// Visual excerpt for reference Ray ray = Camera.main.ScreenPointToRay(Input.mousePosition); RaycastHit hit; if (Physics.Raycast(ray, out hit, maxSelectionDistance, selectableLayers)) { currentSelection = hit.transform; Renderer r = currentSelection.GetComponent(); if (r != null) { originalColor = r.material.color; r.material.color = Color.yellow; } }
Misconception

Highlighting modifies a material; consider material instancing if multiple objects share one material to avoid changing all instances.

Testing steps
  • Assign objects to SelectableObjects layer.
  • Attach script to Camera and set selectableLayers in Inspector.
  • Run, hover to see yellow highlight, click to log the object name and hit point.
Example card
If the ray hits the top face of a cube, hit.point provides the world coordinate where an effect or tooltip should appear.

screens.title: Ground Detection with GroundChecker
screens.subtitle: A small, reliable pattern to determine if a character is grounded

narration.text: Ground detection commonly uses a short downward ray to check whether a character is standing on a collider in the Ground layer. The GroundChecker example casts a ray from a point near the character's feet downward by groundCheckDistance. Using FixedUpdate is a good practice because physics checks synchronize with physics simulation. If Physics. Raycast returns true within the specified distance against the groundLayer mask, set isGrounded to true; otherwise, set it to false. Visualize the check with Debug. DrawRay, using green when grounded and red when not, so you can see the status change in the Scene view. Important details include offsetting the ray origin slightly below the character's pivot to ensure the ray starts inside or at the bottom of the character collider, and choosing a proper distance that accounts for small gaps and animation movement. A common trap is using too small a distance that misses ground during small hops, or using Update instead of FixedUpdate which can produce inconsistent timing with physics. Try the mini-challenge: gate a jump action using isGrounded so the character only jumps when this boolean is true. How will you choose the origin offset and distance for your character capsule?

keyIdea.title: Ground check pattern
keyIdea.text: Cast a short ray downward from the character, use a Ground layer mask, and visualize results with Debug.DrawRay to toggle isGrounded reliably.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › GroundChecker Pattern
FixedUpdate and ray origin
Use FixedUpdate for physics checks. Offset the ray origin slightly below the character pivot to ensure robust contact detection.
public float groundCheckDistance = 0.1f; public LayerMask groundLayer; public bool isGrounded { get; private set; } void FixedUpdate() { Vector3 rayOrigin = transform.position + Vector3.down * 0.05f; if (Physics.Raycast(rayOrigin, Vector3.down, out RaycastHit hit, groundCheckDistance, groundLayer)) { isGrounded = true; } else { isGrounded = false; } Debug.DrawRay(rayOrigin, Vector3.down * groundCheckDistance, isGrounded ? Color.green : Color.red); }
Why this matters

A reliable ground check prevents mid-air jumps and keeps player controls consistent during physics updates.

Testing and tuning
  • Adjust groundCheckDistance to tolerate small gaps and animation frames.
  • Verify layer assignment and groundLayer mask in the Inspector.
  • Watch Debug.DrawRay color changes in the Scene view during play.
Mini challenge
Use isGrounded to allow jumping only when true. Observe the boolean flipping during contact transitions.

screens.title: Linecast and Other Casts
screens.subtitle: When a ray is not enough: linecast, sphere, capsule, and box casts

narration.text: A simple ray is precise but effectively one-dimensional. When you need thicker detection or an explicit start and end, other casts are preferable. Physics. Linecast takes a start and end point and checks the segment between them; it is a convenience form when you already know endpoints. SphereCast casts a sphere along a direction and is useful for detection with volume — for example to check slightly wider shots or enemies in a cone. CapsuleCast and BoxCast extend this idea with capsule or box volumes and are handy for character sweep tests and anticipating collisions during movement. Use these when a thin ray misses targets because of small offsets or when you want to detect collisions of a moving bounding volume. An example: use SphereCast for a shotgun spread detection or to ensure a character doesn’t clip corners. A common misconception is to replace all rays with sphere casts; thicker casts cost more computation, so prefer rays when precision is desired. Decide based on the shape of the object you're trying to detect and performance constraints. Which cast will you pick when testing a wide melee attack?

keyIdea.title: Choosing a cast
keyIdea.text: Use Linecast for fixed endpoints, SphereCast for thicker detection, and Capsule/BoxCast for sweep checks when volume matters.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Linecast & Volume Casts
Linecast
Linecast(start, end, out hit, layerMask) checks a segment directly between two points and is useful when you already know both endpoints.
SphereCast
SphereCast(origin, radius, direction, out hit, maxDistance, layerMask) casts a moving sphere and detects objects that intersect that volume during the sweep.
When to choose a volume
  • When objects can be missed by a thin ray due to size or offset.
  • For sweep checks to detect collisions along movement paths.
  • When you need area-like detection for attacks or proximity checks.
Performance note

Volume casts are more expensive than rays. Use them only when necessary and limit their frequency.

screens.title: Practical Use Cases
screens.subtitle: Shooting, AI line of sight, object placement and other real examples

narration.text: Raycasts are ubiquitous in gameplay systems. For shooting mechanics, cast a ray from the gun barrel or camera forward and, if it hits an enemy, apply damage and spawn an impact effect at hit. point oriented with hit. normal. For AI line of sight, the agent casts a ray toward the player's position; if the ray returns true and hits the player, the path is unobstructed. For object placement, cast from the camera toward the scene to find a valid surface point and use hit. point to place the object cleanly on the surface. Ground checks rely on downward rays. Each scenario follows a similar architecture: determine ray origin and direction, pick a max distance, configure LayerMask to include relevant layers, perform the cast, and react based on RaycastHit fields. A misconception is making the ray originate from the wrong pivot; ensure origin aligns with the intended perspective like the weapon muzzle or camera center. Another pitfall is using overly large maxDistance values that detect unintended objects behind the intended target. Always choose sensible ranges and masks for predictable behavior. Which gameplay case will you prototype first using this architecture?

keyIdea.title: Common patterns
keyIdea.text: Shooting, AI sight, placement, and ground checks all follow the same raycast architecture: origin, direction, mask, distance, and reaction to RaycastHit.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Practical Use Cases
Shooting (instant hit)
Cast a ray from muzzle or camera. If hit, apply damage using hit.transform and show impact at hit.point aligned with hit.normal.
AI Line of Sight
Cast a ray from the agent to the player's position. If the ray hits the player and not an obstacle, the agent has sight.
Placement & Grounding
Use camera rays to find a placement point on scene geometry, and short downward rays to confirm grounding for characters.
Example
Place a turret at hit.point found by a camera ray, and rotate it to face targets based on hit.normal or transform positions.

screens.title: Debugging and Common Mistakes
screens.subtitle: What typically goes wrong and how to verify ray behavior

narration.text: Debugging raycasts often comes down to three issues: missing colliders, incorrect LayerMask configuration, and wrong ray direction or origin. First, ensure the target has a Collider. If a ray passes through, it may be because the object lacks a collider. Second, check the LayerMask: if your mask excludes the layer, the ray will ignore the object silently. Third, verify origin and direction by visualizing rays with Debug. DrawRay or Debug. DrawLine in the Scene view; use different colors to represent expected versus actual direction or distance. Normalize direction vectors when using maxDistance so the scale is consistent. Also guard access to RaycastHit fields by checking the boolean result of Physics. Raycast. For performance, reduce the frequency of expensive casts and restrict masks. A useful debugging workflow is to temporarily set the mask to include all layers and draw the debug ray; once you confirm geometry and direction, tighten the mask and hide debug lines. Remember to remove or conditionally compile heavy debug drawing in release builds. After following these checks, the ray should behave predictably. Which of these checks will you add as a quick test next time a ray fails?

keyIdea.title: Debug checklist
keyIdea.text: Verify colliders, confirm LayerMask, visualize with Debug.DrawRay, normalize direction, and guard access to hit data.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Debugging Raycasts
Quick checks
  • Does the target have a Collider component?
  • Is the object's layer included in your LayerMask?
  • Is the direction normalized and pointing where you expect?
  • Are you reading RaycastHit only after a successful cast?
Visual verification
Use Debug.DrawRay(ray.origin, ray.direction * maxDistance, color) to see the exact ray in the Scene view. Toggle colors based on condition to make state obvious.
Performance tip

Limit ray frequency and scope. Use masks and reasonable maxDistance to avoid expensive checks in dense scenes.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Build and Test
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step lab to implement MouseSelector and GroundChecker

narration.text: Follow a step-by-step lab to consolidate your learning. Start by creating a new 3D scene with a plane at the origin and several primitives scattered on it. Create a new layer named SelectableObjects and assign your primitives to that layer. Add a Camera and attach the MouseSelector script; in the Inspector set selectableLayers to SelectableObjects and pick a sensible maxSelectionDistance. Run the scene and move the mouse; objects should highlight in yellow when the ray hits them. Next, add a character capsule with a Ground layer for floor and a GroundChecker script attached to the character. Set groundCheckDistance to around 0.1 and assign the groundLayer. Enter play mode and observe the isGrounded boolean toggling in FixedUpdate. Use Debug. DrawRay to observe rays in the Scene view: red when not grounded, green when grounded. Experiment by moving objects to different layers and adjusting distances to see how masks and ranges affect detection. Finally, try a mini-challenge: allow the character to jump only if isGrounded is true. This activity teaches you how to connect ray results to game logic and debug them visually.

keyIdea.title: Lab focus
keyIdea.text: Build the MouseSelector and GroundChecker, tune LayerMask and distances, and verify behavior with Debug.DrawRay in the Scene view.

Lab: Selection and Ground Check

  2. Create layer SelectableObjects and assign it to your primitives.
  3. Add a Camera and attach the MouseSelector script.

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential points. First, raycasting is a non-physical query that detects colliders by casting an invisible line and returns a RaycastHit only on success. Second, construct rays with an origin and a normalized direction, call Physics. Raycast with an out RaycastHit, and always check the boolean result before using hit data. Third, LayerMask is a bitmask used to include or exclude layers; use the Inspector to reduce errors and pass masks into ray calls for performance and correctness. These condensed concepts are the building blocks for selection, shooting, line-of-sight checks, ground detection, and placement. Keep a short checklist: colliders present, masks configured, direction normalized, and Debug. DrawRay used to verify behavior. With those habits you will avoid the most common mistakes and implement reliable interactions quickly. Key Concepts — What to Remember means raycasts are queries; check returned booleans; use layermask to filter; visualize rays for debugging.. In practical terms, compact reminders for quick reference. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Core reminders
keyIdea.text: Raycasts are queries; check returned booleans; use LayerMask to filter; visualize rays for debugging.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Key Concepts
Raycasting
Instant, non-physical queries that return hit info when intersecting colliders.
RaycastHit
Contains collider, transform, point, normal, and distance — use only after a successful cast.
LayerMask
Bitmask that filters which layers a cast will hit; set in Inspector for clarity.
Summary takeaway

Use raycasts as efficient queries, read hit data only after success, and filter results with LayerMask. Visualize rays when verifying behavior.

screens.title: Core Reminders
screens.subtitle: Three concise concept cards for quick recall

narration.text: A final quick memory aid. First: always check the boolean returned by Physics. Raycast before accessing RaycastHit, to avoid null access and unexpected errors. Second: use LayerMask to narrow down hits to relevant layers; this both prevents false positives and reduces computation. Third: pick the right cast for the job — ray for precise lines, sphere or box casts for volume sweeps when objects could be missed. Keep these three checks in your mental checklist when implementing interaction features. They will save debugging time and make your interactions more robust and performant. keyIdea.title: Three quick checks
